fragments.body:
The Little Opry is a red barn at the railroad crossing, and it has never once been just a barn. On Saturdays the floor is cleared for the square dance. Most nights it's a club — music, laughter, the occasional scandal. And on Sunday mornings the same tables and chairs line up in neat rows for the preacher, then get shoved aside by evening for the dancers' stomping boots again.

The remarkable thing isn't that one building does all this. It's that nobody in Blind Eye finds it remarkable. The fiddle player is the same man at all three. He tunes the same way, nods the same way, and has never once acknowledged that the room changed around him.
fragments.thread: Ask Ida Noe what she heard from the back pew last Sunday. She won't tell you either.
fragments.title: Three nights, one barn

fragments.body:
Two years ago, on a Sunday evening, the tables would not budge. Six men pushed. The tables held their church formation like they'd grown roots through the floorboards. The square dancers waited an hour, then danced around them, which everyone agreed was the finest dance in living memory.

By morning the tables had returned to the walls on their own. Nobody saw it happen. Nobody has tried to explain it, which in Blind Eye is the same as explaining it.
fragments.thread: Horace Hand says his clocks all stopped at 6:40 that evening. All of them. He reset every one to seven minutes off, like always.
fragments.title: The night the tables wouldn't move
